extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history, philosophy, and the social sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and methodological criteria for studying history and social phenomena — how to detect laws of social progress, use statistical evidence, distinguish kinds of causes, and assess the role of individuals and governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual state conditions social progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of human progression in all respects will mainly depend on the order of progression in the intellectual convictions of mankind — the state of knowledge at any time is the limit of the industrial improvements possible at that time; similarly for the fine arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating causes of material or cultural improvement, prioritize changes in knowledge, beliefs, and speculative faculties as primary determinants; other dispositions (moral, economic) often depend on intellectual condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical changes are preceded by changes in prevalent beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Every considerable change historically known to us in the condition of any portion of mankind, when not brought about by external force, has been preceded by a change, of proportional extent, in the state of their knowledge, or in their prevalent beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In causal accounts of social change, look for prior transformations in opinion or knowledge as plausible antecedent causes; use long-range historical evidence to establish such sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comte's three stages of speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculation ... has, on every subject of human inquiry, three successive stages: (1) explains phenomena by supernatural agencies, (2) by metaphysical abstractions, and (3) confines itself to ascertaining their laws of succession and similitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the intellectual development of a topic by these stages to analyze the maturity of explanatory frameworks; use this as a heuristic for interpreting historical shifts in modes of explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Historical Method to derive laws of social order and progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The method characterized is that by which the derivative laws of social order and of social progress must be sought; by its aid we may determine what artificial means may be used to accelerate natural progress or guard against dangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt systematic historical inquiry aiming to detect regularities (laws) governing social phenomena; apply derived laws cautiously to policy or reform recommendations, recognizing scope and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity/causation of human actions (not fatalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of the Causation of human actions asserts only that men's actions are the joint result of the general laws and circumstances of human nature, and of their own particular characters; it is not an overruling fatality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat human volitions as causally determined by identifiable general and particular causes without conflating this with fatalism; explanations should seek those causes rather than invoke mysterious necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical regularity en masse indicates causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts of statistics show that events apparently capricious in individuals (murders, suicides, accidents, undirected letters) occur with surprising regularity in proportion to population; this regularity en masse corroborates the law of causation for human conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregate statistical patterns as empirical evidence for regular causal influences in social phenomena; include representative examples and caution about period/area limitations when generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish general causes from special (individual) causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Each particular act depends on general circumstances and on causes special to the individual; the collective aggregate separates the effect of general from special causes, showing the net result of the former while leaving the strength of special causes undetermined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis, explicitly separate population-level (systemic) factors from individual-level idiosyncratic causes; use sufficiently large fields/cycles to let special causes average out when seeking general laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require wide temporal and spatial scope to detect laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Because progress of knowledge and changes in opinions are very slow, the general order of sequence cannot be discovered from the examination of less than a very considerable part of the duration of social progress; it is necessary to take into consideration the whole of past time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer long-range, broad geographic data when inferring regularities in social evolution; be skeptical of strong generalizations based on short timespans or limited locales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring moral unchangeability from short-range statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Some have inferred from regularity in recurrence of events that moral qualities are little capable of being improved; but statistics compiled within narrow geographical limits and few years eliminate moral causes that vary across ages/locations, so such inferences are unwarranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When statistical averages appear stable, test whether moral or cultural variables were held constant by the sample frame; compare across ages/countries/regions before concluding moral traits are invariable or unimportant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation is compatible with effective human agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the laws of social development may be universal, human will can convert these into instruments of its designs; human and social facts are more modifiable than physical facts, so individual and collective volitions can be powerful causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume social laws preclude effective intervention; evaluate policies and actions as causal agents that can alter trajectories, especially when they harness underlying general conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional individuals and governments matter (celerity and direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptional individuals in important positions, and the opinions and purposes of those who compose a government, may be indispensable links in the chain of causation; the existence of great men often decides whether there shall be any progress and particularly its celerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical explanations, assess both systemic prerequisites and the role of singular actors/governments in accelerating or redirecting change; recognize their effects may be contingent on pre-existing general conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical prediction is conditional, not absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical science authorizes not absolute, but only conditional predictions. General causes count for much, but individuals also produce great changes and color history long after their death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame forecasts about social development as conditional on known general causes and contingent on unpredictable exceptional actors or combinations; avoid deterministic assertions of inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in generalizations about sequence and form of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: There is need of great flexibility in our generalizations about the order of succession of social states: different portions of mankind, under different circumstances, have developed in different manners and forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for multiple developmental paths; avoid one-size-fits-all models of social evolution and test generalizations against cross-cultural and contextual variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science can trace preparatory conditions even if not specific agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Science can trace through past history the general causes which had brought mankind into that preliminary state which, when the right sort of great man appeared, rendered them accessible to his influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accounting for pivotal historical changes, seek the systemic preconditions that made extraordinary impacts possible (intellectual climate, institutions), even if the precise timing or person cannot be predicted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate governmental acts by long-term and indirect effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments often produce important results which they did not foresee; comparatively enlightened rule (Spain example) may arrest decline and have long-term consequences beyond immediate, visible outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess governmental interventions not only for immediate measurable outcomes but for longer-term indirect influences on institutions, culture, and subsequent developments; historical impact may be delayed or diffuse.
